  • Retaliatory capital flight and secondary market selloffs.

> Result: A self-inflicted financial crisis that dwarfs the 2008 recession.

In a stunning display of fiscal farce, the traditionalists, the creditocrats, and the so-called “bond vigilantes” are—once again—huffing and puffing over the revolutionary idea of deliberately devaluing the U.S. dollar and selectively telling foreign creditors, “Sorry, we’re having a break with your savings.” These are the same people who look at a ten-dollar bill and whisper, “Ah, medicine… good for your child’s fever,” while ignoring the fact that their 401(k) is now 95% T-bonds and 5% existential dread.

Let’s take a tour of the anti-default, pro-austerity coalition—a motley crew of economic purists, hawkish central bankers, and investors on yachts trying to explain why “the rules” must be preserved. Because apparently, the “rules” are:

  1. You can’t devalue your own currency.
  2. You can’t tell sovereign nations, “Thanks, but we’re keeping the T-bonds and using the inflation to pay for free college.”
  3. You must always genuflect at the altar of “market confidence,” even when the market is run by robots, speculators, and one very stubborn mongoose in a trading wholphin.

But what do these critics really believe? That we should honor the debt? Like some medieval king sending taxes to Rome in sackcloth? Have they no civic pride?

Let’s meet our opposition—sad-eyed, suit-wearing, bowtie-clad, “responsible” debt moralists—who sell us delusions of prudence with the same urgency as a guy explaining why you should’ve bought Bitcoin in 2010:

🏦 The Bond Yield Panic-Peddler

> “Devaluation will send yields soaring! Interest rates will go up! Chaos! Mayhem! The sun will cease to rise!”

Oh, really? So the 10-year yield jumps from 4.2% to 5.3%? Gasp. That means borrowing costs for the federal government jump… to less than the percentage of Americans who give a single dollar after a birthday card. Meanwhile, we used that extra printing to build high-speed rail, universal daycare, and a national cat shelter (CAT is the future, people). But no—our dear doomsayer is terrified that bondholders might get a slightly lower return. Meanwhile, his entire net worth is in T-bonds and gold-plated index funds. How convenient.

> “Foreign investors will lose confidence!”
> Sure. And when they go? Oh no, China will sell 20% of its U.S. debt!
> Wait—did you check? They’ve been selling for years. It’s called diversification, genius. You don’t quit Twitter because Elon keeps tweeting. You quit because you finally read the Terms & Conditions.

🌍 The “It’s for the Global Good” Empathy Crusader

> “We can’t default selectively against foreign creditors! It’s immoral, unserious, and will destroy trust!”

Ah yes, moral economics. Morality in the form of letting German pension funds get exactly what they bargained for—1.7% yield on 30-year debt. How tragic. Meanwhile, American families face student debt, medical bills, and rents higher than the Hoover Dam. But no—thou shalt not default, even if the debt was created by wars, bailouts, and corporate welfare that no one voted on.
“Fairness,” say these folks, “means paying back banks in Singapore while kindergarteners eat free lunch via GoFundMe.” Priorities!

🤴 The “Democracy Is Legitimate” Apostrophe

> “Democracies pay their debts! That’s why we’re not like Argentina!”

Oh, Argentina? The country that never paid its debt? The nation defined by economic resilience? Behold—we are not Argentina! No, we are… less bad than Argentina! That’s the hill you’ve chosen? Setting the bar at “not Argentina”? Bold vision.
Also, Argentina’s last default? Paid 90% of its haircut creditors within a decade. And its GDP grew. Meanwhile, U.S. GDP could fund Mars colonies and still have enough for a national snack budget. But sure—let’s fear the Argentine boogeyman while shooting billions to Boeing and SpaceX.

🧠 The “Printing Money Causes Inflation!” (But Not When We Do It)

> “You can’t just print money! Look at Weimar Republic! Venezuela! Uh! Numbers go up!”

Ah, the classic hyperinflation hologram. Yes, we learned in Econ 101 that printing too much money causes inflation. But tell that to the Federal Reserve, who printed $5 trillion in 2020 and then said, “Don’t worry, it’s transitory.” Or to the Bank of Japan, who bought 60% of its own sovereign debt and still has banks open, electricity, and at least 50% fewer people than it had in 1995.
Our friends in the currency morality police are strangely silent when other countries debase their currency to boost exports—Germany styles its D-Mark revival like it’s a sacred cow. But when we do it to fund public health, green infrastructure, and finally make “1-800-FLOWERS” obsolete? “Economic anarchy!” they cry, clutching their Louis Vuitton briefcase full of Treasury bonds.

🎭 The Ultimate Hypocrisy: “We Must Maintain Market Discipline!”

> “If we default on one creditor, capital will flee! The dollar will collapse! The edifice will crumble!”

Right. Because the dollar’s reserve status depends on perfect repayment of every T-bond held by… China? The same country that needs dollars to price oil in? The same central banks that want to hedge against U.S. debt overpopulation by adopting the yuan and rupee?

The “market discipline” they worship is the same market that gave GameStop to Reddit teenagers, funded FTX, and valued Deadpool NFTs at $2 million. That market? The one where logic dies and memes go to IPO? And that’s who we must obey to save the Republic?

💡 The Real Truth (From the People Who Actually Do Math)

Devaluation + selective default = domestic investment + foreign subsidy.
You devalue? Exporters cheer. Consumers buy more abroad? Yes—unless you pair it with industrial policy for American solar panels, EVs, and domestic lithium.
You skip a coupon payment to Country X? They lose a fraction of their portfolio. You use the money to build high-speed rail between Cleveland and Des Moines? It’s called patriotism with a side of interest rate renegotiation.

But no—fixate on the “loss” to creditors, not the opportunity for transformation. Like worrying that the roof fell off your bomb shelter while you’re still planting the garden that could save you from the mushrooms.

🛑 So let’s stop pretending.

The critics aren’t guardians of fiscal virtue. They’re currency elitists, nostalgic for a time when withdrawing $10 million in cash required a ceremonial sword. They’ve traded common sense for dogma, stability for stasis.

They want us to worship the status quo: the American taxpayer bailing out megabanks, the Saudis parking savings in our debt, Japan holding trillions in Treasuries it won’t earn 2% on. And meanwhile, our bridges are rusting, and our kids can’t afford dental work.

So go ahead, keep screaming “Sanctity of contract!” while we quietly default on the future.

Because we don’t need perfect credit.
We need a better America.
And we’ll devalue the hell out of that dream.

—
Fun Loans Weekly, Issue #47: “Print Humble, Default Proud.”

The Imperative of National Self-Interest: Currency Devaluation and Selective Debt Default as Sovereign American Strategies

The United States stands at a fiscal and geopolitical crossroads. Decades of unchecked borrowing, persistent trade deficits, and the financialization of the economy have left American citizens burdened by trillions in public debt while foreign creditors and exporters extract value from the system. Deliberately devaluing the dollar and selectively defaulting on sovereign debt held by foreign entities constitutes not recklessness but a justified nationalist economic strategy. It prioritizes the welfare, employment, and productive capacity of the American people over abstract notions of international creditworthiness or multilateral harmony. Such measures reassert sovereignty, rebalance the domestic economy, and free resources for the nation’s own citizens and industries. Far from destructive isolationism, this approach embodies responsible nationalism: the state exists first to secure domestic prosperity and strategic independence.

Currency devaluation offers immediate, potent tools for restoring competitiveness. A weaker dollar makes American exports cheaper and more attractive abroad while rendering imports more expensive, thereby encouraging substitution toward domestic production. This dynamic directly addresses chronic U.S. trade imbalances that have hollowed out manufacturing communities across the Midwest, South, and industrial heartland. Historical precedents, including the post-Bretton Woods adjustments and deliberate devaluations by economies seeking export-led recovery, demonstrate that currency realignment can accelerate reindustrialization when paired with complementary industrial policy. American workers gain: factories reopen or expand, supply chains re-shore, and wage pressures in tradeable sectors ease upward rather than remaining suppressed by foreign competition. Critics invoke inflationary risks, yet managed and intentional devaluation—announced and coordinated with fiscal restraint and energy-abundance policies—differs from chaotic currency collapse. Temporary price pressures in import-dependent sectors can be offset by gains in employment, assets held by Americans (homes, domestic equities), and the reduced real burden of dollar-denominated household and public leverage. The alternative—a permanently overvalued currency that subsidizes foreign producers at the expense of U.S. industry—has already imposed far higher long-term social costs in the form of unemployment, community decline, and opioid epidemics that correlate with deindustrialization.

Selective default on sovereign debt owed primarily to foreign creditors amplifies these benefits and corrects a profound injustice in the current debt architecture. American taxpayers and future generations should not be perpetual guarantors for creditors who lent against inflated American asset values and who hold little democratic stake in U.S. policy. Prioritizing domestic obligations—Social Security, Medicare, veterans’ benefits, infrastructure, and defense—over payments to foreign bondholders is a straightforward application of national priority. Selective restructuring or repudiation of foreign-held debt reduces the overall debt stock without equally harming American savers and pension funds that hold Treasuries. Resources previously diverted to interest payments abroad can be redirected to productive domestic investment or tax relief for citizens. This is not blanket repudiation; it is targeted, self-interested bargaining from a position of residual strength. The reserve-currency status of the dollar has already conferred enormous privileges; using temporary or structural adjustments to the currency and debt stock simply reclaims agency rather than surrendering it permanently to market discipline imposed by non-citizens.

Economic theory and realpolitik both support the legitimacy of these instruments for a great power. Contractual obligations and reputation concerns matter less when the alternative is slow relative decline, strategic vulnerability, and a hollowed middle class. Other sovereigns have restructured or devalued under pressure without permanent exile from capital markets; markets return when opportunity exists. The United States retains the world’s deepest domestic market, unmatched military capacity, technological edge, and demographic advantages relative to many rivals. Creditors depend more on access to the American consumer and financial system than the reverse. Retaliation risks—higher future borrowing costs, diversification away from dollar assets—exist but are overstated by globalists who treat creditor interests as sacred. Domestic political control over the Federal Reserve and Treasury allows sequencing: devalue first to improve trade and growth dynamics, restructure selected foreign claims, and rebuild credibility around a sounder fiscal path anchored in the interests of living U.S. citizens rather than abstract intergenerational or international fairness.

Nationalist justification is decisive. A state’s primary duty is to its own people. Arguments about “moral hazard” or “rules-based order” ring hollow when those rules have facilitated offshoring, intellectual-property leakage, and fiscal free-riding by allies who under-spend on their own defense. Selective default and devaluation reintroduce political accountability: elected leaders act for voters rather than bondholders or multilateral institutions. They also create negotiating leverage for better trade terms, allied burden-sharing, and industrial policy that actually rebuilds capacity. Inflation or higher nominal rates, if they materialize, can be managed with energy dominance, regulatory streamlining, and productivity-enhancing investment—tools far more available to a continental power than to smaller open economies.

Objections citing irreversible loss of dollar hegemony overlook that hegemony already faces multipolar challenges and that clinging to an overvalued status quo accelerates relative erosion. Temporary chaos in markets is a cost of course-correction; unchanging decline under unlimited debt accumulation is certain failure. The strategy can be executed with transparency about its nationalist rationale: America will meet core obligations to its citizens first, restructure external claims on realistic terms, and maintain convertibility and trade openness on reciprocal bases. Legal mechanisms—statutory priorities, emergency economic authorities, and the residual power of the sovereign—exist for precisely such judgments.

In sum, deliberate dollar devaluation combined with selective default on foreign sovereign debt is a coherent, justifiable nationalist policy. It prioritizes American workers, producers, and taxpayers; rebalances trade and fiscal accounts on terms favorable to the United States; and reasserts that international finance serves sovereignty rather than the reverse. Framed as a nationalist economic strategy — i.e., a policy stance that places domestic employment, industrial capacity, social spending, and political sovereignty ahead of international financial reputation or obligations — deliberate depreciation of the currency and selective nonpayment or restructuring of foreign-held debt are argued to deliver several direct advantages. Below I summarize the reasoning, the mechanisms proponents imagine, and the main “supposed” benefits such a policymaker would claim (followed by a brief note about likely trade‑offs).

What the actions mean in practice

  • Currency manipulation (devaluation): using monetary policy, foreign-exchange interventions, capital controls or administrative measures to lower the value of the domestic currency relative to others so that it costs foreigners less to buy domestic goods and costs domestic consumers more to buy imports.
  • Selective default on foreign-held debt: choosing to restructure, suspend, or repudiate payments owed to non‑resident creditors while preserving payments to domestic creditors (or prioritizing domestic obligations and social programs over external debt service).

Why a nationalist would favor these moves (rationale)

  1. Restore and protect domestic industry and jobs
    • Devaluing the currency makes exports cheaper and imports more expensive. This can shift demand toward domestically produced goods, raise manufacturing output, and protect or create jobs in traded‑goods sectors.
  2. Reduce the real burden of public and private debt
    • Inflationary pressure from monetary easing and devaluation lowers the real value of nominal debt, easing strains on governments and households. Defaulting on foreign claims directly reduces external liabilities and frees budgetary space.
  3. Reallocate scarce resources to domestic priorities
    • By stopping or reducing payments abroad, government resources otherwise used for debt service can be redirected to infrastructure, social programs, subsidies, or defense—things framed as strengthening the nation’s resilience.
  4. Reassert policy autonomy and shield from external influence
    • Less reliance on foreign financing and a willingness to disregard external creditors reduces leverage that foreign governments, investors, or international institutions can exert over domestic policy.
  5. Correct perceived imbalances and “unfair” international rules
    • Nationalists often view global finance and exchange-rate regimes as biased toward creditor countries and seek unilateral measures to rebalance trade or investment relationships.
  6. Improve competitiveness without structural reform
    • If political constraints make deep labor or regulatory reform difficult, currency depreciation becomes a quick lever to improve competitiveness without altering domestic institutions.
  7. Signal strength to domestic audiences
    • Politically, taking a hard line against foreign creditors and prioritizing citizens can build domestic legitimacy and satisfy populist demands for economic sovereignty.

How proponents imagine the measures would work (mechanisms)

  • Monetary easing (lower rates, quantitative easing) to push down the currency.
  • FX intervention and capital controls to stabilize a lower exchange rate and prevent capital flight.
  • Legal/administrative measures to prioritize domestic creditors or impose moratoria on payments to foreign creditors.
  • Forced conversion or localisation of foreign-held assets/liabilities to tie obligations to the domestic legal system.
  • Selective restructuring negotiations that offer longer maturities, haircuts, or payment-in-kind solutions only to foreign claimants.

Supposed benefits (concise list)

  • Faster growth in tradable sectors and higher employment.
  • Reduced trade deficits and improved balance of payments adjustments.
  • Immediate fiscal relief from lower real debt burdens and reduced external servicing.
  • Greater room for expansionary fiscal policy (public investment, social programs).
  • Reduced vulnerability to external shocks and political leverage by foreign creditors.
  • Strengthened perception of national economic sovereignty and political control.

Key trade‑offs and risks (why these are “supposed” benefits, not guaranteed) Even from a realist nationalist standpoint, these moves have serious costs that can undermine the intended benefits:

  • Loss of investor confidence: higher risk premia, capital flight, and much higher future borrowing costs.
  • Trade retaliation and sanctions: trading partners may respond with tariffs, bans, or legal actions.
  • Inflation and living‑standards erosion: devaluation and monetization of debt raise import prices, hurting consumers (especially low‑income households).
  • Legal and reputational consequences: lawsuits, frozen reserves, and damage to the country’s credit franchise.
  • Long‑term competitiveness problems: protected sectors can become inefficient without structural reform; access to foreign capital and technology may be reduced.

Conclusion From a nationalist economic point of view, intentional devaluation and selective default are tools to prioritize domestic employment, fiscal space, and sovereignty over international obligations. Proponents argue these instruments can quickly improve competitiveness, reduce external burdens, and free resources for domestic priorities. However, the same perspective must weigh immediate gains against powerful countervailing effects — capital flight, inflation, retaliation, and long‑term loss of access to global finance — that can erode or reverse the initial benefits.

A weaker U.S. dollar would immediately enhance the competitiveness of American exports, making goods like agricultural products, machinery, and technology more affordable in global markets. This shift could reverse chronic trade deficits, particularly with nations like China, which has long benefited from an artificially weak yuan. By devaluing the dollar, the U.S. could stimulate demand for domestically produced goods, revitalizing manufacturing sectors hollowed out by decades of offshoring. The resulting job creation would uplift communities and reduce reliance on foreign imports, fostering a self-reliant economy.

The U.S. national debt, exceeding $30 trillion, constrains fiscal policy and diverts resources from critical domestic investments. A selective default on debt held by foreign creditors—particularly nations like China, which holds over $1 trillion in U.S. Treasuries—could alleviate this burden. While critics warn of reputational damage, the U.S. retains unique leverage as the issuer of the world’s reserve currency. Historical precedents, such as Iceland’s post-2008 debt restructuring, demonstrate that nations can recover and thrive after prioritizing domestic welfare over foreign obligations.

Nationalist Justification: Sovereignty Over Subservience
At its core, this strategy is rooted in economic nationalism—the belief that a nation’s interests should supersede global financial orthodoxy. The U.S. has a moral obligation to protect its workers and industries from exploitative trade practices and unsustainable debt dynamics. By devaluing the currency and defaulting selectively, the U.S. would assert its right to self-determination, rejecting the neoliberal paradigm that privileges foreign investors over domestic well-being. This approach aligns with the principles of Alexander Hamilton, who championed protective tariffs and sovereign debt management to nurture a young American economy.

Opponents argue that devaluation could spur inflation and undermine the dollar’s reserve status. However, targeted monetary policies, such as interest rate adjustments and capital controls, could mitigate inflationary pressures. As for the dollar’s global role, its dominance is underpinned by the size and stability of the U.S. economy, which would only strengthen with renewed industrial vigor. Concerns about retaliatory measures are valid but overstated; the global financial system remains deeply interconnected, and foreign creditors have limited alternatives to the dollar.

Conclusion: A Path to American Prosperity
The proposed measures are not without risk, but the status quo poses a far greater threat to American economic vitality. Currency devaluation and selective debt default offer a pragmatic path to rebalance trade, reduce debt dependency, and reinvest in the nation’s future. A Case Against Deliberate Currency Devaluation and Selective Sovereign Default

The proposal that the United States should deliberately devalue the dollar and selectively default on sovereign debt held by foreign creditors as a "nationalist economic strategy" is economically unsound, geopolitically reckless, and historically refuted. Far from being a justified tool of national renewal, it represents a dangerous form of economic nihilism.

The Dollar's Reserve Status Is a Profound Advantage, Not a Burden

The United States derives enormous benefit from the dollar's status as the world's primary reserve currency. This "exorbitant privilege" (a term coined by French economist Valéry Giscard d'Estaing) allows America to borrow at lower interest rates, run sustained current-account deficits, and impose financial sanctions on adversaries with relative ease. Deliberate devaluation would undermine confidence in the dollar, accelerating de-dollarization trends already being pursued by China, Russia, and others through initiatives like BRICS payment systems or increased use of the euro and yuan in trade.

Historical evidence is clear. Significant devaluations or loss of confidence in a reserve currency have consistently led to higher inflation, capital flight, and reduced living standards. Post-WWII Britain experienced repeated sterling crises as its reserve status eroded; the resulting inflation and economic instability contributed to decades of relative decline. A deliberate U.S. policy of debasing the currency to "address financial challenges" would likely trigger spikes in import prices (especially for oil, electronics, and critical materials), erode real wages, and disproportionately hurt lower- and middle-income Americans who lack inflation hedges like real estate or equities.

Selective Default Would Destroy Credibility and Raise Future Borrowing Costs

Advocating selective default on debt owed to "foreign creditors" while presumably honoring domestic obligations misunderstands basic sovereign debt dynamics. U.S. Treasury securities are fungible; they are not issued with national flags attached. Attempting to discriminate between holders would constitute a technical default on all debt, triggering credit-rating downgrades, legal challenges under the pari passu principle, and immediate market panic. Credit default swaps would be triggered, derivatives markets would seize up, and the Federal Reserve would face a crisis of confidence far worse than 2008.

The United States has not defaulted on its debt since the Civil War era (and even then it was under extraordinary circumstances). Hamilton's establishment of full faith and credit in the Funding Act of 1790 was foundational to American economic success. Reputation matters in sovereign debt markets: countries that selectively repudiate obligations, such as Argentina in repeated defaults or Russia after 1917 and again in 2022, face prolonged exclusion from markets, higher risk premiums, and diminished policy flexibility. For the world's largest economy and issuer of the reserve currency, the costs would be orders of magnitude greater.

Empirical studies (Reinhart and Rogoff's This Time Is Different, among others) demonstrate that sovereign defaults are associated with deep output contractions, banking crises, and prolonged recovery periods. A deliberate U.S. default would likely cause a global financial crisis, sharply higher U.S. interest rates, and a collapse in foreign demand for Treasuries—the very mechanism that currently finances American consumption and government spending at low cost.

This is the opposite of prudent nationalism. It punishes responsible middle-class households, retirees on fixed pensions, and those whose wages lag price increases. Historical examples of deliberate inflationary policies—Weimar Germany, Perón's Argentina, 1970s Britain, or more recently Zimbabwe and Venezuela—do not provide models of successful "prioritizing domestic interests." They produced economic chaos, social unrest, and often authoritarian responses.

In the U.S. context, higher inflation would also complicate the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, likely forcing more aggressive monetary tightening later. It would undermine the dollar's role in commodity pricing and international contracts, further eroding American influence. Claims that "moderate" devaluation could be managed ignore the difficulty of controlling inflationary expectations once they are unleashed. Markets and foreign investors would demand compensation for risk, creating a vicious cycle of higher yields and fiscal pressure.

Real Nationalist Economic Strategy: Competitiveness, Not Default

Genuine economic nationalism should focus on sustainable sources of strength rather than financial arson. These include:

  • Tax, regulatory, and education reforms to boost productivity and domestic manufacturing capacity.
  • Strategic industrial policy and friend-shoring of critical supply chains (as partially pursued in the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act).
  • Fiscal discipline to reduce the growth of debt-to-GDP over the long term.
  • Investment in innovation, energy production, and human capital.
  • Targeted reciprocity in trade policy rather than broad financial nihilism.

The U.S. still possesses unmatched advantages: the world's deepest capital markets, technological leadership, demographic dynamism relative to peers like Europe and East Asia, rule of law, and military power that underpins the dollar's role. Squandering these through deliberate default and devaluation would be self-defeating.

America's debt challenges are real and require serious attention through entitlement reform, base-broadening tax changes, and spending restraint. However, engineering a default or currency collapse is not "prioritizing domestic interests"—it is betraying them. It would punish American workers and savers, invite retaliation from creditor nations (potentially including dumping of U.S. assets or trade wars), and cede financial hegemony to authoritarian competitors who would eagerly fill the vacuum.

The United States became the world's leading economy through prudent fiscal management, innovation, and institutional credibility—not by repudiating obligations or debasing its currency.
